text: 9 Lecture 9 9.1 Cramer’s rule Theorem 9.1 (Cramer’s rule). Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ) be invertible and b ∈ F n. Then the solution x = (x1, x2, . . . , xn)t to Ax = b is given by: xi = det(Ai(b)) det(A) , for i = 1, 2, . . . , n. Proof. Let x = (x1, x2, . . . , xn)t be the unique solution to Ax = b. Then, Ax = x1v1 + x2v2 + · · · + xnvn = b. Therefore det(Ai(b)) = ∑n j=1 xj det(Ai(vj)) = xi det(A) and hence xi = det(Ai(b)) det(A) . Example 9.2. Consider the equation { a11x1 + a12x2 =b1 a21x1 + a22x2 =b2 If A = (a11 a12 a21 a22 ) is invertible, then the unique solution to this equaiton is x1 = det ( b1 a12 b2 a22 ) det ( a11 a12 a21 a22 ) = b1a22 − b2a12 a11a22 − a21a12 , x2 = det ( a11 b1 a21 b2 ) det ( a11 a12 a21 a22 ) = a11b2 − a21b1 a11a22 − a21a12 . Proposition 9.3. Let M be an n × n matrix of the form M = ( A B 0 C ) , where A ∈ Mp×p(F ), B ∈ Mp×(n−p)(F ), C ∈ M(n−p)×(n−p)(F ) and 0 is a matrix of all zeros. Show that det(M ) = det(A) det(C). Proof. If C is singular, then rank C < n − p. Then the last n − p rows of (A B 0 C ) are linearly dependent. Hence M is singular. So det(M ) = 0 = det(A) det(C). If C is invertible, we consider the function D(A) = det(C)−1 det ( A B 0 C ). Then D(A) satisfies (i), (ii) in Definition 7.12 since det does. Moreover, by applying Proposi- tion 8.14 repeatedly, we get D(I) = det(C) −1 det ( I B 0 C ) = det(C)−1 det(C) = 1. Thus by Theorem 8.1, we have D(A) = det(A). 50 Remark 9.4. One can similarly show that det      A1 ∗ · · · ∗ 0 A2 · · · ∗ ... ... . . . ... 0 0 · · · An      = det(A1) . . . det(An). where Ai are square matrices whose diagonal aligns with the diagonal of the whole matrix. This should be compared with Proposition 8.14. 9.2 Polynomials This section is an introduction to polynomial theory. We only need the conclusions. For a proof, see [1, Chapter 9]. For a proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental theorem of algebra. Definition 9.5. Let F be a field. The set of all polynomials in one variable x with coefficients in F is denoted by F [x]. Note that there is no restriction on the degree here. In other words, F [x] = ∪∞ n=1Pn(F ). A general element of F [x] has the form f (x) = anxn + · · · + a1x + a0, where a0, . . . , an ∈ F , and n ∈ N. If f (x) ∈ F [x] is nonzero, its degree, denoted deg(f ), is the highest power of x with nonzero coefficient. We define deg(0) = −∞ by convention. A polynomial f (x) ∈ F [x] is called monic if its leading coefficient is 1. Theorem 9.6. Given polynomials f (x), g(x) ∈ F [x] with g(x) ̸= 0, there exist unique polynomials q(x), r(x) ∈ F [x] such that: f (x) = q(x)g(x) + r(x), with deg(r) < deg(g). This is called the Euclidean division. Example 9.7. x3 − 1 = (x2 + x + 1)(x − 1). Definition 9.8. Let f (x), g(x) ∈ F [x]. We say that g(x) divides f (x), written g(x) | f (x), if there exists q(x) ∈ F [x] such that f (x) = q(x)g(x). Definition 9.9. Let f (x) ∈ F [x], and let α ∈ F . We say that α is a root (or zero) of f if f (α) = 0. Proposition 9.10. α ∈ F is a root of f (x) if and only if (x − α) | f (x) in F [x]. Definition 9.11. Let p(x) ∈ F [x] be a nonzero polynomial of degree n. We say that p(x) splits in F if it can be written as a product of linear factors, that is, p(x) = a(x − λ1)(x − λ2) · · · (x − λn), 51 for some a ̸= 0 and λ1, . . . , λn ∈ F . One can also write it as p(x) = a(x − λ1) k1(x − λ2)k2 · · · (x − λm)km where λ1, . . . , λm are distinct roots of p and ki is the multiplicity of λi. Theorem 9.12 (Fundamental theorem of algebra). Let p(x) ∈ C[x]. Then p(x) splits in C. Example 9.13. Let p(x) = ax2 +bx+c where a, b, c ∈ R. Then p(x) = a(x−λ1)(x−λ2) in C[x] where λ1 = −b + √b2 − 4ac 2a , λ2 = −b − √b2 − 4ac 2a here you can take the square root of any real number since if b2 − 4ac ≥ 0 then it’s the usual square root, if b2 − 4ac < 0, then √b2 − 4ac = √4ac − b2√−1 = √4ac − b2i. For example x2 + 1 does not splits in R since it has no roots in R. However, x2 + 1 = (x − i)(x + i) splits in C and the roots are ±i. Also x3 − 1 = (x − 1)(x2 + x + 1) does not splits in R since x2 + x + 1 has no roots in R. However, x3 − 1 = (x − 1)(x − λ1)(x − λ2) in C where λ1 = −1+ √3i 2 and λ2 = −1− √3i 2 . Note that λ2 1 = ( −1+ √3i 2 )2 = 1−2 √3i−3 4 = −1− √3i 2 = λ2. So the above formula is also written as x3 − 1 = (x − 1)(x − ω)(x − ω2) where ω = λ1. Definition 9.14. Let z = x + yi be a complex number x, y ∈ R. The complex conjugate is the complex number ¯z = x − yi. x is called the real part of z and y is called the imaginary part of z. We write x = Re z and y = Im z. (Note that the imaginary part Im should not be confused with the image im.) We have the following properties for complex conjugates: zw = ¯z ¯w and z + w = ¯z+ ¯w. Let A = (aij) ∈ Mm×n(C). We define the complex conjugate matrix ¯A = (aij) ∈ Mm×n(C) and Re A = (Re aij) ∈ Mm×n(R) and Im A = (Im aij) ∈ Mm×n(R). By the properties above, it’s not hard to show that AB = ¯A ¯B and A + C = ¯A + ¯C for A, C ∈ Mm×n(C), B ∈ Mn×p(C). Example 9.15. If A = (1 − i 1 + i 1 1 ) , then ¯A = (1 + i 1 − i 1 1 ), Re A = (1 1 1 1 ) and Im A = ( −1 1 0 0 ) . Lemma 9.16. Suppose p(x) ∈ R[x] and we regard it as a polynomial in C[x]. If z ∈ C is a root of p i.e. p(z) = 0, then ¯z is also a root of p i.e. p(¯z) = 0. Proof. Since p(x) = anxn + · · · + a0 ∈ R[x], ai = ai p(¯z) = an(¯z)n + · · · + a1 ¯z + a0 = anzn + · · · + a1z + a0 = ¯0 = 0. Proposition 9.17. For any p(x) ∈ F [x], there is a field extension E of F i.e. a field E containing F , such that p(x) splits in E. The smallest such field E is called the splitting field of p(x). 52 9.3 Eigenvalue and eigenvectors Let T : V → V be a linear transformation. We would like to find a basis such that [T ] β β is the simplest. The simplest possible matrix is the diagonal matrix diag(λ1, . . . , λn). Although this is not always achievable, if we do have such a basis β = (v1, . . . , vn), then the vi satisfies the special property that T (vi) = λivi for 1 ≤ i ≤ n. Definition 9.18. We say that λ ∈ F is an eigenvalue of T and v ∈ V is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ if v ̸= 0 and T v = λv. A linear transformation T : V → V is diagonalizable over F if there is a basis β of V such that [T ] β β = diag(λ1, . . . , λn). The set of all eigenvalues of T is called the spectrum of T denoted by σ(T ). In matrix language, λ ∈ F is an eigenvalue of A and v ∈ F n is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue λ if v ̸= 0 and Av = λv. A ∈ Mn×n(F ) is diagonalizable over F if there is P ∈ Mn×n(F ) invertible such that P −1AP = diag(λ1, . . . , λn). Remark 9.19. The word spectrum comes from quantum mechanics since the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian operator are the energy of light emitted from a black body. So the study of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a linear operator is also called spectral theory. Proposition 9.20. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ). Then λ is an eigenvalue and v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ if and only if det(λI − A) = 0 and 0 ̸= v ∈ ker(λI − A). Proof. Since Av = λv, we have (λI − A)v = 0 i.e. v ∈ ker(λI − A). Since v ̸= 0, λI − A is not invertible. Hence det(λI − A) = 0. Definition 9.21. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ). The polynomial pA(x) = det(xI − A) ∈ F [x] is the characteristic polynomial of A. λ is an eigenvalue of A if and only if λ is a root of pA(x). The subspace E(λ, A) = ker(λI − A) is called the eigenspace with eigenvalue λ. The dimension dim E(λ, A) ≥ 1 is called the geometric multiplicity of λ. The maximal integer k such that (x−λ)k | pA(x) is called the algebraic multiplicity of λ. The following four examples are all possible situations that one may encounter when finding the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix. Example 9.22. This is an example where the matrix is diagonalizable. A = ( 7 −10 5 −8 ) ∈ Mn×n(R) pA(x) = det(xI − A) = (x − 7 10 −5 x + 8 ) = (x − 7)(x + 8) + 50 = x2 + x − 6 = (x − 2)(x + 3). The eigenvalues of A are λ1 = 2, λ2 = −3 and both of algebraic multiplicity 1. Solving 0 = (2I − A)v = ( −5 10 −5 10 ) v we have v = c ( 2 1 ) for c ∈ R. 53 Solving 0 = ((−3)I − A)v = ( −10 10 −5 5 ) v we have v = c ( 1 1 ) for c ∈ R. Thus λ1 = 2 is an eigenvalue with eigenvector ( 2 1 ) and λ2 = −3 is another eigenvalue with eigenvector (1 1 ). The geometric multiplicities of λ1, λ2 are both 1. If we write P = ( 2 1 1 1 ) then AP = P ( 2 −3 ) i.e. P −1AP = diag(2, −3). Example 9.23. This is an example where A is not diagonalizable since the field is too small to contain all eigenvalues of A. A = ( −1 2 −1 1 ) ∈ M2×2(R) pA(x) = det(xI − A) = ( x + 1 −2 1 x − 1 ) = (x + 1)(x − 1) + 2 = x2 + 1. There is no root of pA(x) in R which means A has no eigenvalues and eigenvectors over R. In particular, A is not diagonalizable over R. Example 9.24. This is an example where we enlarge the field F to contain all eigen- values of A and A becomes diagonalizable in the enlarged field. A = ( −1 2 −1 1 ) ∈ M2×2(C) pA(x) = det(xI − A) = (x + 1 −2 1 x − 1 ) = (x + 1)(x − 1) + 2 = x2 + 1 = (x − i)(x + i). The eigenvalues of A in C are λ1 = i, λ2 = −i both of algebraic multiplicity 1. Solving 0 = (iI − A)v = ( i + 1 −2 1 i − 1 ) v we have v = c (1 − i 1 ) for c ∈ C. Solving 0 = ((−i)I − A)v = ( −i + 1 −2 1 −i − 1 ) v we have v = c ( 1 + i 1 ) for c ∈ C. Thus λ1 = i is an eigenvalue with eigenvector ( 1 − i 1 ) and λ2 = −i is another eigenvalue with eigenvector ( 1 + i 1 ) . The geometric multiplicities of λ1 = i, λ2 = −i are both 1. If we write P = ( 1 − i 1 + i 1 1 ) then AP = P (i −i ) i.e. P −1AP = diag(i, −i). Remark 9.25. Suppose we regard A ∈ Mn×n(R) as a matrix in Mn×n(C). If λ ∈ C is a complex eigenvalue with nonzero imaginary part, then ¯λ is also an eigenvalue of A by Lemma 9.16. In fact if v is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue λ, then ¯v is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue ¯λ. This is because if Av = λv then A¯v = ¯A¯v = Av = λv = ¯λ¯v. So in practice, we only need to compute half of the eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Remark 9.26. In Example 9.23, A is not diagonalizable over R. In Example 9.24, we enlarge R to C and A becomes diagonalizable. The price to pay is that the matrix P is 54 a complex matrix, not a real matrix. In general, the issue of the field F not being large enough to contain all eigenvalues can be resolved by Proposition 9.17. Example 9.27. This is an example where A is not diagonalizable since there are not enough eigenvectors. A = ( −1 −4 1 3 ) pA(x) = det(xI − A) = ( x + 1 4 −1 x − 3 ) = (x + 1)(x − 3) + 4 = x2 − 2x + 1 = (x − 1)2. λ = 1 is the only eigenvalue of A. It has algebraic multiplicity 2. Solving 0 = (I − A)v = ( 2 4 −1 −2 ) v we have v = c ( −2 1 ) for c ∈ R. Thus λ = 1 is an eigenvalue with eigenvector (−2 1 ) . Note that there is only 1 linearly independent eigenvector and the geometric multiplicity is 1. Remark 9.28. In this example, pA(x) already splits in R[x], but there is not enough eigenvectors to diagonalize A i.e. geometric multiplicity < algebraic multiplicity. The indiagonalizability is essential and cannot be overcome by choosing a larger field. To see that A is not diagonalizable from another perspective, suppose A is diagonalizable. Then P −1AP = diag(λ1, λ2). In this case, pA(x) = (x − 1)2 and we must have λ1 = λ2 = 1. That means P −1AP = I and A = P P −1 = I which is not possible.
